stories.headline: Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate Democratic leader; Trump says it will be 'hard' to work with Schumer

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) has led Senate Democrats since 2017, as both minority and majority leader.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), 67, launched a challenge to Schumer for Senate Democratic leader after Democrats' midterm wins in November.
Van Hollen said on NBC's 'Meet the Press' his support is 'north of 15' senators, short of the 28 votes needed to win.
Fox News reported Schumer has 15 senators in his camp.
Van Hollen's publicly identified backers include Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan.
Senate Democrats and senators-elect will hold a leadership vote in December to choose the next majority leader.
President Trump wrote on Truth Social Sunday it would be 'very hard' to work with Schumer as majority leader, calling him 'one of the worst' leaders and predicting he will 'fail again.'
Rahm Emanuel said Schumer should commit to stepping down as leader after the next Congress, according to ABC News.
Van Hollen confirmed on 'Meet the Press' that he will not run for president in 2028, regardless of the leadership race's outcome.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen argues the caucus wants change, that Democrats are 'on probation' with voters, and that 'you don't earn people's trust by going back to business as usual.'
Sen. Chuck Schumer has said he welcomes 'discussion about the future of our caucus' and maintains he has 'the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader.'
Rahm Emanuel says Schumer should commit to stepping down as leader after the next Congress.
President Trump predicts it will be 'very hard' to work with Schumer as majority leader, calling him 'one of the worst' leaders in history and saying he will 'fail again.'
Van Hollen says his backing is 'north of 15' and growing.
Schumer maintains he already has 'the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader.'
The December caucus vote will determine who leads Senate Democrats into the new Congress, settling the contest between Schumer and Van Hollen for control of the party's agenda in the chamber.

ladder.analysis: This is an internal Democratic power struggle triggered by the party's strong midterm showing, which puts Senate Democrats on track to hold the majority in January and makes the question of who leads them — Schumer or a challenger — consequential for control of the chamber's agenda. The leadership vote is decided within the Democratic caucus, with 28 votes needed among senators and senators-elect to win. Van Hollen represents the more progressive wing of the party and has drawn support from figures like Bernie Sanders, while Schumer's camp argues his decade of leadership helped deliver the recent wins now fueling Democratic confidence.

stories.headline: Hakeem Jeffries' past Jerusalem comments resurface as he prepares to become House speaker

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

The nomination positions Jeffries to become the first African American speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.
Jeffries won a secret-ballot vote to remain House Democratic Caucus leader by a 251-11 margin.
Jeffries grew up in Brooklyn.
Jeffries worked as a corporate litigator at Paul, Weiss.
Jeffries worked in-house at CBS before entering politics.

facts: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker on a Wednesday vote, positioning him to become the first African American speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.
Jeffries won the secret-ballot vote to remain House Democratic Caucus leader by a 251-11 margin.

Jeffries grew up in Brooklyn, worked as a corporate litigator at Paul, Weiss and later in-house at CBS before entering politics; his mother taught Sunday school at Cornerstone Baptist Church in Bedford-Stuyvesant.
In a 2020 interview with AIPAC that recently resurfaced, Jeffries said New Yorkers consider Jerusalem the city's '6th Borough' and described Israel as living in a 'tough neighborhood.'

In a July letter to colleagues, Jeffries wrote that 'a meaningful change in direction is needed' on U.S.-Israel security arrangements, while also condemning Rep. Thomas Massie's (R-Ky.) effort to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military aid to Israel.
At least eight incoming members with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America, plus Reps.-elect Brad Lander and Scott Wiener, have called for ending or embargoing U.S. aid to Israel.
Jeffries has not used the term 'genocide' to describe the Israel-Hamas war and has rejected a full cutoff of U.S. aid to Israel.
ladder.analysis: Hakeem Jeffries is on track to become the first Black speaker of the House, capping a career that moved from corporate law to Brooklyn politics. According to New Yorker writer Jason Zengerle, Jeffries is a cautious, consensus-seeking leader who has generally avoided ideological labels — except on Israel, where he has long been identified as a strong supporter. That identification is now colliding with a broader Democratic shift: as more members, including a growing DSA-aligned bloc and some established lawmakers, push to cut or condition aid to Israel, old comments like Jeffries' 2020 'sixth borough' remark are resurfacing and drawing scrutiny. Jeffries himself has shifted rhetorically since the Gaza war began in 2023, calling for changes to U.S.-Israel security arrangements, but he has stopped short of embracing the harsher positions some in his party now hold.

DSA-aligned incoming Democrats, along with Reps.-elect Brad Lander and Scott Wiener, have called for ending or fully embargoing U.S. military and economic aid to Israel.
rep: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) pushed an amendment to cut $3.3 billion in U.S. military aid to Israel from a State Department appropriations bill, a move Jeffries publicly opposed.

ladder.steelman: The resurfaced comments highlight that Jeffries occupies a shrinking middle ground on Israel — more supportive than his party's rising progressive wing but more critical than his earlier career suggested — making the issue a genuine test of his ability to hold together an increasingly divided caucus.
ladder.implications: As speaker, Jeffries will likely face recurring pressure from progressive Democrats to harden his stance on Israel aid, even as he seeks to preserve caucus unity and mainstream support ahead of future votes on security assistance and messaging legislation.

stories.headline: FBI investigates hack of National Crime Information Center database

claims.text: US media reports, citing people briefed on the matter, say the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database.
The NCIC is used by federal, state and local law enforcement to check warrants, criminal histories, gun background checks, missing-persons and sex-offender records.
The NCIC feeds data to patrol-car computers nationwide via roughly 56 state terminals and over 100,000 users.
Investigators have not yet determined the breach's entry point.
Investigators have not confirmed whether any data was stolen, viewed, or altered.
There is no confirmed outage of the system.
In September, a group called ShinyHunters breached the FBI's job-portal website.
ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on roughly 38,000 bureau employees.
Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested Oct. 8 in connection with the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters.
President Trump, asked about the NCIC breach in a Fox News interview with Kayleigh McEnany, said he had 'just heard' about it.
President Trump called the NCIC breach 'not good.'
President Trump added 'maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise.'
The FBI did not respond to requests for comment from BBC.
The FBI did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News.
A Government Accountability Office report found 17 of 22 federal agencies were not in compliance with federal cybersecurity regulations.
The White House's National Cyber Director, Sean Cairncross, was fired this week.
The NCIC is one of the most widely used law-enforcement databases in the country.
The NCIC feeds real-time information to officers during traffic stops, background checks and fugitive searches.
Cybersecurity experts say any compromise — especially one that altered rather than merely exposed data — could carry operational safety risks for police.
The reported breach follows a September hack of the FBI's job portal by the extortion group ShinyHunters.
The reported breach follows a GAO finding that most federal agencies fail basic cybersecurity compliance standards.
The reported breach follows the firing of the White House's top cyber official.
The reported breach follows a separate reported intrusion into a USDA payment system.
None of these events have been publicly tied together by officials.
Investigators have not yet said what, if anything, was taken or changed in the NCIC breach.
Across outlets, the consistent and uncontested throughline is that investigators still do not know the scope or impact of the breach.
Investigators still do not know whether any records were viewed, stolen, or altered.

The FBI's investigation will need to determine whether any records were altered in ways that could affect officer safety or the integrity of criminal records.

facts: US media reports, citing people briefed on the matter, say the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database.

The NCIC is used by federal, state and local law enforcement to check warrants, criminal histories, gun background checks, missing-persons and sex-offender records, and feeds data to patrol-car computers nationwide via roughly 56 state terminals and over 100,000 users.
Investigators have not yet determined the breach's entry point or confirmed whether any data was stolen, viewed, or altered; there is no confirmed outage of the system.

This marks the second reported cyberattack on the FBI in recent months: in September, a group called ShinyHunters breached the FBI's job-portal website and claimed to have stolen personal information on roughly 38,000 bureau employees.
Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested Oct. 8 in connection with the FBI's investigation into ShinyHunters, according to court records and law-enforcement sources.

President Trump, asked about the NCIC breach in a Fox News interview with Kayleigh McEnany, said he had 'just heard' about it and called it 'not good,' adding 'maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise.'
The FBI did not respond to requests for comment from either BBC or Fox News.

A Government Accountability Office report found 17 of 22 federal agencies were not in compliance with federal cybersecurity regulations, and the White House's National Cyber Director, Sean Cairncross, was fired this week.
ladder.analysis: The NCIC is one of the most widely used law-enforcement databases in the country, feeding real-time information to officers during traffic stops, background checks and fugitive searches, which is why cybersecurity experts say any compromise — especially one that altered rather than merely exposed data — could carry operational safety risks for police. The reported breach lands amid a broader pattern of strain on federal cyber defenses: it follows a September hack of the FBI's job portal by the extortion group ShinyHunters, a GAO finding that most federal agencies fail basic cybersecurity compliance standards, the firing of the White House's top cyber official, and a separate reported intrusion into a USDA payment system. None of these events have been publicly tied together by officials, and investigators have not yet said what, if anything, was taken or changed in the NCIC breach, but together they have intensified scrutiny of the federal government's capacity to secure sensitive systems.
ladder.steelman: Across outlets, the consistent and uncontested throughline is that investigators still do not know the scope or impact of the breach — whether any records were viewed, stolen, or altered — making it premature to draw conclusions about harm until the FBI's incident response is complete.
ladder.implications: The FBI's investigation will need to determine whether the intrusion originated from a compromised user credential, a state terminal, or a third-party vendor, and whether any records were altered in ways that could affect officer safety or the integrity of criminal records. The episode, coming alongside other recent federal cyber incidents and compliance shortfalls identified by the GAO, is likely to sharpen congressional and public attention on the resourcing and oversight of federal cybersecurity defenses going forward.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU, others reject deal lacking fossil fuel mention
body: United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Sunday after nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement, with the European Union and several other nations rejecting a final draft text that omitted any explicit reference to fossil fuels. The breakdown marked the first time the annual UN climate summit has ended without a deal since Copenhagen in 2009.

The proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, would have acknowledged for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold set by the 2015 Paris Agreement. However, key oil- and gas-producing countries opposed mentions of 'fossil fuels' in the text, and the revised draft also dropped a $120 billion target for funds to help poorer countries adapt to climate change. The final version referred to earlier decisions, including the 2023 Dubai agreement, but did not explicitly mention fossil fuels and retained provisions on carbon capture and storage, a technology promoted by some oil-producing nations but criticized by environmental groups.

The European Union formally rejected the deal, with EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra telling reporters after walking out of the talks, 'That is not acceptable.' Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, said the bloc would not endorse a decision 'that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel.' After the EU walked out, other countries including Panama, the Marshall Islands, Norway, and Vanuatu also objected. The Marshall Islands delegation said, 'We have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas.'

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed 'a very profound frustration,' saying, 'I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.' He criticized powerful fossil fuel interests for obstructing climate action, accusing them of distorting scientific evidence, delaying policies, and prioritizing profits. The Least Developed Countries group, representing 44 nations most vulnerable to climate change, said, 'We struggled to find meaningful outcomes that respond to the priorities of the most vulnerable countries like us. We cannot afford to see backsliding.'

COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkiye's environment minister, said, 'We did everything we could. You should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase.' He added that no new text would be proposed. Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister and COP31 president of negotiations, called the collapse 'very disappointing,' noting that 'an obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned. Other parties insisted that if it was mentioned, they would veto.' Russia's delegate argued that shrinking oil and gas supplies would lead to 'dirtier types of fuel and energy poverty,' while Saudi Arabia said it believed 'climate change requires all solutions on the table.' The United Kingdom's lead climate negotiator, Kate Hughes, said the draft 'moves us backwards on the science,' and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the summit 'sought to confront hard truths' but failed to build consensus.

stories.headline: Bahrain says Iran strikes industrial facility as tanker struck in strait
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Bahrain’s air defence systems intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks on Saturday, but a civilian industrial facility on Sitra Island was struck, causing a fire and damage, the interior ministry said. No casualties were reported initially, though the ministry later said a Bahraini citizen with disabilities and a Pakistani resident were injured, the latter critically. The attacks ended a weeks-long lull in the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.

Two tankers were also hit in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). One was struck by an unknown projectile and another sustained damage in its engine room. Iran claimed that a vessel caught fire after hitting a mine in a restricted zone and separately said its Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had shot down a US drone over Qeshm Island, the 20th such drone it had downed. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) rejected Iranian claims that an F-16 fighter jet was attacked, stating all American military aircraft in the region were safe.

The IRGC claimed responsibility for attacking two US bases in Bahrain, Sheikh Isa and Juffair, in response to what it called US illegal actions. Iran also unveiled a new missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-propellant missiles simultaneously. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted a Houthi drone launched toward Riyadh, and the Saudi Foreign Ministry issued a strong condemnation of the Iranian attack on Bahrain, affirming full solidarity. The UAE and Jordan also condemned the strike as a violation of Bahrain’s sovereignty and a dangerous escalation.

Iran is reportedly preparing to send 14 oil tankers through the US naval blockade, raising the prospect of a direct confrontation with American warships and threatening energy security across the Arabian Gulf. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has already fallen 65% below pre-war levels. The US, which has been escorting ships through the strait, faces the central question of whether Washington will forcibly stop the tankers. The American Embassy in Bahrain warned citizens of increased threats from Iranian-backed Houthis and Iranian attacks targeting US assets in the region.

Australia’s embassy in Saudi Arabia advised its citizens not to travel to the kingdom, citing volatile security, drone and missile attacks on airports and oil facilities, and significant air travel disruptions. In Lebanon, the army arrested three people for smuggling 264 kilograms of explosives from Syria. Israel’s defence circles are examining the scenario of a preemptive Iranian strike, believing Tehran could attack first if it concludes a joint US-Israeli assault is imminent. The IRGC warned that Iranian airspace remains a “red line” and that any violation would be met with a “harsh, decisive and powerful response.”

stories.headline: Stock market correction deepens; analysts debate bounce vs. further losses
body: The stock market sell-off has deepened, with the Nasdaq Composite firmly in correction territory and the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 approaching similar thresholds, according to multiple financial outlets. As of the Nov. 19 market close, the Nasdaq was down 13.5% from its all-time high of 27,722.75 set on Oct. 6, while the Dow had fallen 9.7% from its high and the S&P 500 was down 8.2%. The speed of the decline has been notable: both the Nasdaq and S&P 500 were at all-time highs in early October, and the Nasdaq has dropped 10.1% in just three weeks. A further fall to 22,178.20 on the Nasdaq would mark a 20% decline from its peak, meeting the common definition of a bear market. Some analysts argue that given the rapid descent from a high just six weeks ago, such a drop could also be classified as a crash.

The sell-off has been particularly severe in certain sectors and stocks. Nvidia, which was the world's most valuable company for most of this year, has lost roughly a third of its value in three weeks, accelerated by the sudden resignation of its founder and CEO of over 33 years, Jensen Huang. The Motley Fool's Daniel Foelber noted that while Nvidia's decline may have gone too far, the business is 'definitely weaker without Huang,' and he shifted his stance on the stock from buy to hold pending clarity on national security risks, restructuring, and leadership. Other pockets of the market have seen crash-like declines: Taiwan was hit hardest among country ETFs, down 23.2% in dollars last week, followed by South Korea down 13.7%, according to Yardeni QuickTakes. Gold fell to $3,555 per ounce, its lowest since September 2025, and copper dropped 9.9% to $5.48 a pound. Even Bitcoin has undergone rapid declines.

Despite the sell-off, analysts are divided on the outlook. Yardeni QuickTakes described the sell-off as a buying opportunity, noting that global profits are still booming and forward earnings remain at record highs both in the U.S. and overseas. The U.S. MSCI's forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 17.7, while the emerging markets MSCI trades at just 7.9, its lowest since the Great Financial Crisis. Yardeni wrote, 'We said valuations were at or near a bottom. They went lower. We still think the panic selling will abate soon.' MarketWatch highlighted a timing model from Norm Fosback's 'Seasonality Timing System,' which has a strong long-term track record and suggests the market has an upside bias for the next two weeks. However, the Motley Fool cautioned that volatility could be swifter and more severe due to widespread access to information, high-frequency trading, and zero-fee brokerages, and that index concentration—Nvidia alone made up around 8% of the S&P 500 at its peak—amplifies moves.

Bonds rallied worldwide as investors fled stocks, sending yields lower. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield fell 24 basis points to 4.92% from 5.16% a week earlier, according to Yardeni. The dollar has been a safe haven, with the DXY rising to 103.8 from an intraday low of 101.1 on Nov. 4. In Asia, South Korea's stock market has crashed even as its forward earnings are up 325.1% year-to-date, cutting its forward P/E to a record low of 3.2. Yardeni noted that investors are betting analysts' estimates are too high due to concerns that a slowdown in the AI buildout will depress memory chip prices, but South Korean exports soared 93.9% year-over-year in October to a record, led by shipments to China and the U.S. In Japan, headline CPI rose to 2.4% year-over-year in October, above the Bank of Japan's 2.0% target, raising the odds of a rate hike.

For investors, the Motley Fool recommended buying high-quality stocks and ETFs during periods of intense volatility, but cautioned against assuming every beaten-down stock is cheap. Foelber pointed to ASML, a leader in semiconductor equipment, as a clearer buying opportunity than Nvidia, and suggested beaten-down growth stock ETFs like the Vanguard Growth ETF and Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF for broad exposure. He advised investors to 'only buy stocks you are OK with holding even if volatility continues to intensify.' The stakes are high as the crucial holiday shopping period approaches, with some stocks already in bear market territory.

stories.headline: Ravens offered Colts a fourth-round pick for Daniel Jones before Indianapolis released him
body: The Baltimore Ravens offered the Indianapolis Colts a fourth-round draft pick and a conditional fifth-round selection for quarterback Daniel Jones before the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10, according to multiple reports. The proposed deal would have sent a 2027 fourth-round pick to Indianapolis, along with a fifth-rounder that would have been returned to the Colts if Baltimore advanced to the playoffs. The Minnesota Vikings also expressed interest in Jones, but the Colts held onto him, then released him on Friday after a 26-3 loss to the Houston Texans.

Jones, 29, struggled in 11 games for the Colts in 2026, throwing for 1,974 yards, seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions. In the loss to Houston, he completed 12 of 27 passes for 144 yards and an interception. Indianapolis subsequently turned to Anthony Richardson as its starting quarterback. The Colts had told Jones before the deadline that he would remain with the team, and Jones was surprised when he was informed of his release on Friday, a source told OutKick.

The Colts privately said after the trade deadline that they declined the Ravens' offer because they did not believe they were receiving good value in return, according to a league source cited by Fox News. However, the offer was not necessarily final, as there were still days remaining before the deadline. The Ravens eventually traded for Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, giving up a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-rounder in return.

The decision to release Jones without receiving any draft compensation has drawn criticism. The Colts had already traded offensive guard Quenton Nelson, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, and wide receivers Keenan Allen and Josh Downs at the deadline, while holding onto Jones and star running back Jonathan Taylor despite reported offers. The Colts are also responsible for the remainder of Jones' guaranteed salary if he goes unclaimed on waivers, which is expected.

Jones is expected to clear waivers on Monday and is unlikely to sign immediately with another team, according to ESPN and NFL Network. Instead, he and his representatives plan to study the landscape for the right opportunity, particularly if a playoff contender suffers an injury at quarterback. A team signing Jones after he clears waivers could potentially add him for the NFL minimum, as the Colts remain liable for his guaranteed salary.

stories.headline: Wembanyama scores 50 points in 18 minutes, makes history
body: Victor Wembanyama scored 50 points in a 114-91 victory over the New Orleans Pelicans on Saturday night at Frost Bank Center, tying Spurs legend David Robinson for the second-most 50-point games in franchise history with three. Wembanyama finished with 18 rebounds, five blocks and four steals, shooting 20 of 29 from the field. He had 32 points by halftime, outscoring the Pelicans' starters (26) by himself.

The 22-year-old superstar has now recorded three career 50-point outings, matching Robinson's total. Only George Gervin, with five, has more in Spurs history. Wembanyama's performance also marked his second 50-point game of the season; he scored 52 points in a Nov. 4 win over the Dallas Mavericks. Since an 0-2 start, San Antonio (14-3) has gone 14-1.

Wembanyama is the third player since 1973-74 to log at least 50 points, 15 rebounds and five blocks in a single game. After the game, he said in an on-court interview, 'It is very special.' He added with a smile, 'But unlike many of my peers, I'm not very good at stat padding. So I haven't reached it as many times as I should have.'

Actress Selena Gomez was sitting courtside, and Wembanyama acknowledged her presence. 'Of course, I had to show off for Selena, you know,' he said, laughing. Guard Stephon Castle added 19 points for the Spurs, and De'Aaron Fox contributed 10 assists.

The Pelicans (5-13) have lost nine of their last 10 games after a 4-4 start. Guard Jeremiah Fears, 20, led New Orleans with 29 points. Wembanyama is again an NBA MVP candidate, though he faces competition from Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Dončić, who leads the league in scoring at 37.2 points per game and also has two 50-point games this season.

stories.headline: Marquez wins record-equalling eighth MotoGP title
body: Marc Marquez clinched a record-equalling eighth MotoGP championship with an eighth-placed finish in the Portuguese Grand Prix on Sunday. The Spaniard needed to finish in the top nine on his Ducati to secure a second consecutive title and move level with legendary Italian Giacomo Agostini on eight championships.

Marquez started second on the grid and rode cautiously after crashing out in the sprint race on Saturday. Aprilia's Italian rider Marco Bezzecchi, who held a 102-point advantage over Marquez at one stage this season, won Sunday's race, while Marquez's fellow Spaniards Jorge Martin and Raul Fernandez completed the top three.
The 33-year-old was hoisted in the air by his team after crossing the line. This season, Marquez won seven grands prix and 10 sprint races, adding to the 11 grands prix he won in 2025.
Sunday's title was Marquez's eighth in MotoGP and his 10th championship overall, following wins in the 125cc and Moto2 categories earlier in his career.

stories.headline: Nvidia earnings beat expectations but leadership crisis deepens
body: Nvidia reported soaring revenue for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, beating expectations and raising its outlook, even as a public campaign led by Elon Musk and other tech executives pushes for the return of former CEO Jensen Huang. The company’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors on the earnings call, “Hey, we’ve got this,” while Huang himself has said he is prepared to come back, according to a petition circulated by Musk and others. The conflicting signals have created what TechCrunch’s Kirsten Korosec described as “the tale of two Nvidias this week.”

Nvidia’s revenue rose 103% year over year to $115.8 billion in the quarter ended Oct. 25, driven by a 110% jump in data center revenue. The company forecast $130 billion in revenue for the current quarter, an improvement of 91% over the year-ago period, and raised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance to 75% growth, up from a prior expectation of 70%. The Vera Rubin chip platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue last quarter, which Nvidia called “the fastest product ramp in Nvidia’s history.” Management said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply.

Despite the strong financial results, Nvidia faces a deepening leadership crisis. Huang resigned as CEO, and the company is searching for a permanent replacement. Kress, serving as interim CEO, has publicly stated that Huang’s return is not happening, but TechCrunch noted that Nvidia’s stance shifted rapidly: “A week and a half before that [the company said], ‘We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.’” The board appears determined to avoid being forced into a decision by outside pressure, particularly from Musk, and is trying to “present control,” according to Korosec. An investigation into how much and who knew about chips allegedly being sold secretly to China remains ongoing, further complicating any potential return.

On the China front, Nvidia announced it will stop selling its H200 chips in the country, coinciding with the Trump administration tightening export restrictions and closing a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to remotely access chips in data centers set up in Malaysia and elsewhere. Critics estimate that 20% of Nvidia’s business ultimately comes from China through indirect sales, meaning the crackdown could significantly affect the company’s bottom line, though Kress said the company’s “long pipeline” remains strong.

Looking ahead, Nvidia’s improved guidance signals sustained demand for advanced chips, which also benefits ASML Holding, the near-monopoly maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used to manufacture Nvidia’s 3-nanometer and 4-nanometer processors. However, the leadership drama is far from resolved. As TechCrunch’s Anthony Ha put it, “I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.” The board’s steadfastness in quickly shooting down the petitions, Tim De Chant added, “suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside.”
